concepts.topicTitle: Accumulation of Variation and Its Survival Advantage
concepts.label: Accumulation of Variation During Reproduction
concepts.cardText: Inheritance from the previous generation provides both a common basic body design and subtle changes in it for the next generation. The second generation has differences inherited from the first as well as newly created ones. If a single individual reproduces, as in asexual reproduction, the diversity is small: if one bacterium divides and the two resultant bacteria divide again, the four would be very similar, with only very minor differences due to small inaccuracies in DNA copying. If sexual reproduction is involved, even greater diversity is generated. A field of sugarcane shows very little variation, but sexually reproducing animals, including humans, show quite distinct variations.

concepts.topicTitle: Accumulation of Variation and Its Survival Advantage
concepts.label: Survival Advantage of Variation
concepts.cardText: Do all variations in a species have equal chances of surviving in the environment where they find themselves? Obviously not. Depending on the nature of the variations, different individuals will have different kinds of advantages. Bacteria that can withstand heat will survive better in a heat wave. Selection of variants by environmental factors forms the basis for evolutionary processes.

concepts.label: Heredity: Similarity and Difference Between Parents and Child
concepts.cardText: The most obvious outcome of reproduction is individuals of similar design. The rules of heredity determine the process by which traits and characteristics are reliably inherited. A child bears all the basic features of a human being, yet does not look exactly like its parents, and human populations show a great deal of variation. Free and attached earlobes are two variants found in human populations. Both the father and the mother contribute practically equal amounts of genetic material to the child, so each trait can be influenced by both paternal and maternal DNA, and for each trait there will be two versions in each child.

concepts.topicTitle: Mendel's Experiments: Dominant and Recessive Traits
concepts.label: Mendel's Monohybrid Cross: Dominant and Recessive Traits
concepts.cardText: Gregor Mendel grew garden peas using contrasting visible characters such as round or wrinkled seeds, tall or short plants and white or violet flowers. He was the first to keep count of individuals showing a trait in each generation. Crossing a tall plant and a short plant gave first-generation (F1) plants that were all tall, with no halfway 'medium-height' plants: only one of the parental traits was seen. When the F1 tall plants were self-pollinated, one quarter of the second-generation (F2) plants were short. So both the tallness and shortness traits were inherited in the F1 plants, but only tallness was expressed. Mendel proposed that two copies of a factor (now called genes) control a trait. A single copy of T is enough for a tall plant, while both copies must be t for it to be short. T is dominant and t recessive.

concepts.topicTitle: Mendel's Experiments: Dominant and Recessive Traits
concepts.label: Independent Inheritance of Two Traits
concepts.cardText: What happens when pea plants differing in two characteristics are crossed? A tall plant with round seeds crossed with a short plant with wrinkled seeds gives F1 plants that are all tall with round seeds, so tallness and round seeds are dominant traits. When these F1 plants are self-pollinated, some F2 plants are tall with round seeds and some are short with wrinkled seeds, but there are also new combinations: tall with wrinkled seeds and short with round seeds. These new combinations form when the factors controlling seed shape and seed colour recombine to form the zygote. So the tall/short trait and the round/wrinkled seed trait are independently inherited.

concepts.topicTitle: How Traits Are Expressed: Genes, DNA and Proteins
concepts.label: Genes, Proteins and the Expression of a Trait
concepts.cardText: Cellular DNA is the information source for making proteins in the cell. A section of DNA that provides information for one protein is called the gene for that protein. Take tallness as an example: plants have hormones that trigger growth, so plant height can depend on the amount of a particular plant hormone, which depends on the efficiency of the process for making it. If an enzyme important for this process works efficiently, a lot of hormone is made and the plant is tall. If the gene for that enzyme has an alteration that makes the enzyme less efficient, less hormone is made and the plant is short. Thus genes control characteristics, or traits.

concepts.topicTitle: Inheritance from Both Parents and Chromosomes in Germ-cells
concepts.label: Two Sets of Genes and the Role of Chromosomes in Germ-cells
concepts.cardText: If both parents help determine the trait in the progeny, both must contribute a copy of the same gene, so each pea plant has two sets of all genes, one from each parent. Each germ-cell must therefore have only one gene set. If progeny inherited a single whole gene set from each parent, characteristics like R and y would be linked and could not be independently inherited. This is explained by each gene set being present not as one long thread of DNA but as separate independent pieces, each called a chromosome. Each cell has two copies of each chromosome, one from each parent. Every germ-cell takes one chromosome from each pair, either of maternal or paternal origin. When two germ-cells combine they restore the normal number of chromosomes, ensuring the stability of the DNA of the species.

concepts.label: How Sex Is Determined in Different Species
concepts.cardText: Different species use very different strategies to determine the sex of a newborn. Some rely entirely on environmental cues: in a few reptiles, the temperature at which fertilised eggs are kept determines whether the animals developing in the eggs will be male or female. In snails, individuals can change sex, showing sex is not genetically determined. But in human beings the sex of the individual is largely genetically determined: the genes inherited from our parents decide whether we will be boys or girls.

concepts.label: Sex Chromosomes: X and Y in Human Beings
concepts.cardText: Most human chromosomes are paired, with a maternal and a paternal copy, and we have 22 such pairs. But one pair, the sex chromosomes, is not always a perfect pair. Women have a perfect pair, both called X, while men have a mismatched pair with one normal-sized X and one short Y. So women are XX and men are XY. Half the children will be boys and half girls. All children inherit an X chromosome from their mother, whether they are boys or girls, so the sex of children is determined by what they inherit from their father. A child inheriting an X from the father will be a girl, and one inheriting a Y will be a boy.
